blocks.text: A 24-year-old rugby player is tackled with his arm raised and rotated outwards. His shoulder looks squared-off, he cannot move the arm, and there is a coin-sized patch of numb skin over the outer upper arm. The joint has come out of its socket, and a nerve that lies just beneath it has been stretched.

blocks.markdown: Joint stability comes from three sources: the **bony shape** of the articular surfaces, the **ligaments and capsule**, and the **muscles** that cross the joint. Different joints rely on these in different proportions. The hip, with a deep socket, is stable and rarely dislocates without major force; the shoulder and knee depend on soft tissues and are injured much more often. When the limits are exceeded, ligaments are torn (a **sprain**) or the joint surfaces lose contact (a **dislocation**).

rows: Sprain
Stretching or tearing of a ligament; the joint surfaces remain in contact
Ligament fibres (grade I: stretched, grade II: partial tear, grade III: complete tear)
Subluxation
Partial loss of contact between joint surfaces
Capsule and ligaments, usually stretched or partly torn
Dislocation
Complete loss of contact between the articular surfaces
Capsule and ligaments torn; often labrum, cartilage and sometimes bone, with risk to adjacent nerves and vessels
blocks.caption: Comparing sprain, subluxation and dislocation.

blocks.title: Sprain versus dislocation
blocks.text: A sprain is a ligament injury in which the bones of the joint stay in their normal alignment (at least when at rest); the damage is to the ligament. A dislocation is a displacement of the bones so that the articular surfaces no longer meet; it necessarily involves damage to the capsule and the supporting ligaments, and often to other structures, including neighbouring nerves and vessels.

blocks.markdown: **Anterior dislocation of the shoulder.** The glenohumeral joint has a shallow socket and lax capsule, and its weakest part is anteroinferior, where there is no rotator cuff. A force on the abducted, laterally rotated arm (for example a tackle or a fall with the arm outstretched) drives the humeral head forwards and downwards out of the glenoid; it comes to lie in front of the glenoid, below the coracoid process. The **axillary nerve** (C5, C6) is at risk because it leaves the axilla through the **quadrangular space**, passes just beneath the inferior part of the joint capsule and then winds round the **surgical neck** of the humerus beneath deltoid. A head displaced downwards and forwards stretches or compresses the nerve against the humerus. The deficits are weak abduction (deltoid) and numbness over the lower deltoid (regimental badge area).

blocks.title: Explaining nerve injury in dislocation
blocks.prompt: A patient has an anterior shoulder dislocation. After the shoulder is reduced, he cannot abduct the arm beyond the first few degrees and has numbness over the lateral upper arm. Explain this in anatomical terms.

steps.text: The axillary nerve runs below the inferior capsule of the shoulder joint and round the surgical neck of the humerus.
As the humeral head dislocates downwards and forwards, it stretches the nerve, causing a neurapraxia.

Deltoid is paralysed, so abduction is weak beyond the first 15 degrees that supraspinatus provides; the lower deltoid skin is numb because the upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm is a branch of the axillary nerve.

blocks.answer: Stretching of the axillary nerve (C5, C6) by the displaced humeral head.

blocks.markdown: **Other examples.** In a posterior dislocation of the hip, the femoral head is displaced backwards, and the **sciatic nerve** lying behind the hip can be stretched or compressed. A posterior elbow dislocation can injure the ulnar nerve or brachial artery. A dislocation of the lunate may compress the median nerve in the carpal tunnel. In each case the nerve at risk is the one that lies beside the joint in the direction of displacement.

blocks.title: The unhappy triad of the knee
blocks.text: A blow to the outer side of the knee with the foot fixed (a valgus force with rotation) can tear three structures together: the tibial (medial) collateral ligament, the medial meniscus (which is attached to that ligament) and the anterior cruciate ligament. This combination is called the unhappy triad (O'Donoghue triad). The patient has pain, a swollen knee and instability. The cruciate ligaments hold the tibia against sliding forwards (ACL) or backwards (PCL), and the collateral ligaments resist sideways angulation.

rows: Ankle inversion sprain
Anterior talofibular ligament (most often)
Foot forced into inversion and plantarflexion
Pain and swelling over the lateral ankle
Unhappy triad
ACL, tibial collateral ligament, medial meniscus
Valgus blow to the knee with fixed foot
Swelling and instability of the knee
Anterior shoulder dislocation
Anteroinferior capsule; axillary nerve at risk
Abduction and lateral rotation
Flattened shoulder contour, numb lower deltoid
Posterior hip dislocation
Posterior capsule; sciatic nerve at risk
Force on the flexed knee along the femur (dashboard injury)
Shortened, internally rotated limb; risk of sciatic nerve injury
blocks.caption: Examples of ligament injuries and dislocations.

blocks.title: Identify the triad
blocks.prompt: A footballer is struck on the lateral side of the right knee while his foot is fixed. The knee is swollen, the anterior drawer test is positive and valgus stress shows laxity. Which structures are injured?

steps.text: A positive anterior drawer test indicates ACL damage.
Laxity to valgus stress indicates a tibial collateral ligament injury.
The medial meniscus is attached to the tibial collateral ligament, so it is likely to be torn with it.

blocks.answer: ACL, tibial collateral ligament and medial meniscus: the unhappy triad.

items: Sprain: ligament injury, joint surfaces remain in contact.
Dislocation: joint surfaces lose contact; capsule and ligaments are torn.
Anterior shoulder dislocation: axillary nerve at risk.
Unhappy triad: ACL, tibial collateral ligament, medial meniscus.

blocks.title: Check the nerve before and after reduction
blocks.text: Because nerves lie close to joints, always examine the relevant nerve and distal pulses before and after reducing a dislocation. For the shoulder, test deltoid contraction and sensation over the lower deltoid (regimental badge area).

points: A sprain damages ligament fibres without loss of contact between joint surfaces, whereas a dislocation displaces the surfaces and tears the capsule and ligaments.
An anterior shoulder dislocation can injure the axillary nerve (C5, C6), causing weak abduction and numbness over the lower deltoid.
The unhappy triad of the knee comprises the ACL, tibial collateral ligament and medial meniscus.

questions.stem: Which nerve is most at risk in an anterior dislocation of the shoulder?

options.text: Axillary nerve
Radial nerve
Ulnar nerve
Median nerve

distractorRationale.b: The radial nerve is at risk in humeral shaft fractures.
distractorRationale.c: The ulnar nerve is at risk at the elbow.
distractorRationale.d: The median nerve is at risk at the wrist.

questions.explanation: The axillary nerve runs below the inferior shoulder capsule and round the surgical neck of the humerus. A head displaced downwards and forwards can stretch it.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old has a squared-off shoulder after a tackle and numbness over the lateral upper arm. After reduction he cannot abduct beyond the first few degrees. Which muscle is paralysed?

options.text: Deltoid
Supraspinatus
Biceps brachii
Triceps brachii

distractorRationale.b: Supraspinatus is supplied by the suprascapular nerve and initiates abduction.
distractorRationale.c: Biceps is supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve.
distractorRationale.d: Triceps is supplied by the radial nerve.

questions.explanation: Deltoid is supplied by the axillary nerve and carries abduction beyond the first 15 degrees that supraspinatus initiates. Loss of deltoid together with numbness over the lower deltoid indicates axillary nerve injury.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a sprain?

options.text: Stretching or tearing of a ligament with the joint surfaces still in contact
Complete loss of contact between the joint surfaces
A break in the continuity of a bone
Tearing of a muscle from its tendon

questions.correctOptionText: Stretching or tearing of a ligament with the joint surfaces still in contact

distractorRationale.d: This is a muscle or tendon injury.

questions.explanation: A sprain is a ligament injury. A dislocation, by contrast, involves loss of contact between the joint surfaces and damage to the capsule and ligaments.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a subluxation from a dislocation?

options.text: In a subluxation the joint surfaces are only partly displaced
A subluxation involves only the bone
A subluxation is always a fracture
A subluxation involves no ligament injury

questions.correctOptionText: In a subluxation the joint surfaces are only partly displaced

distractorRationale.b: Subluxation involves capsule and ligament stretch or tear.

questions.explanation: A dislocation is a complete loss of contact, whereas a subluxation is partial displacement. Both involve injury to the capsule and ligaments.

questions.stem: Which three structures are injured in the classic unhappy triad of the knee?

options.text: Anterior cruciate ligament, tibial collateral ligament and medial meniscus
Posterior cruciate ligament, fibular collateral ligament and lateral meniscus
Patellar ligament, quadriceps tendon and ACL
Tibial collateral ligament, lateral meniscus and PCL

questions.correctOptionText: Anterior cruciate ligament, tibial collateral ligament and medial meniscus

distractorRationale.b: This lists lateral and posterior structures.
distractorRationale.d: This is not the classic triad.

questions.explanation: The medial meniscus is attached to the tibial collateral ligament, so a valgus blow tears the ligament, the meniscus and the ACL together.

questions.stem: Which force typically causes the unhappy triad?

options.text: A blow to the outer side of the knee with the foot fixed
A blow to the inner side of the knee
Forced hyperflexion alone
A fall on the outstretched hand

questions.correctOptionText: A blow to the outer side of the knee with the foot fixed

distractorRationale.b: This would tend to cause a varus force and lateral structures to fail.
distractorRationale.c: Hyperflexion alone does not produce this triad.
distractorRationale.d: This injures the wrist, not the knee.

questions.explanation: A blow to the outside of the knee with a fixed foot produces a valgus force with rotation. This strains the tibial collateral ligament, medial meniscus and ACL.

questions.stem: Which ligament is most commonly sprained in an inversion injury of the ankle?

options.text: Anterior talofibular ligament
Deltoid ligament
Anterior cruciate ligament
Plantar calcaneonavicular ligament

distractorRationale.b: The deltoid ligament is on the medial side and is injured in eversion.
distractorRationale.c: The ACL is in the knee.
distractorRationale.d: The spring ligament supports the medial arch.

questions.explanation: The anterior talofibular ligament is the weakest of the lateral ankle ligaments and is torn when the foot is forced into inversion. The medial deltoid ligament is stronger.

questions.stem: True or false: in a sprain the joint surfaces lose contact completely.

options.text: True
False

distractorRationale.a: Complete loss of contact is a dislocation, not a sprain.

questions.explanation: In a sprain the ligament is damaged but the joint surfaces remain in contact. Complete loss of contact defines a dislocation.

questions.stem: Explain why anterior dislocation of the shoulder can injure the axillary nerve, and state the resulting clinical findings.
markingGuide: The anteroinferior capsule is the weakest part of the shoulder joint, so the head dislocates forwards and downwards.
The axillary nerve (C5, C6) passes through the quadrangular space below the inferior capsule and winds round the surgical neck of the humerus.
The displaced head stretches or compresses the nerve.
Deltoid is paralysed: weak abduction beyond the first 15 degrees.
Numbness over the lower deltoid (regimental badge area).
questions.explanation: The nerve lies immediately below the joint in the direction of the displacement. The deficit reflects the muscles and skin it supplies.

questions.stem: Compare a sprain with a dislocation in terms of the structures damaged, and describe the unhappy triad of the knee.
markingGuide: Sprain: ligament stretched or torn; joint surfaces remain in contact.
Dislocation: joint surfaces lose contact; capsule and ligaments torn, with possible injury to nerves, vessels, cartilage or bone.
Unhappy triad: anterior cruciate ligament, tibial (medial) collateral ligament and medial meniscus.
Mechanism: valgus force with rotation on a fixed foot.
The medial meniscus is attached to the tibial collateral ligament.
questions.explanation: A sprain is an injury to the ligament alone, whereas a dislocation also involves the capsule and often adjacent structures. The unhappy triad shows how a single force damages several linked structures.
